sections.normalized_html:
By the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Here, the points [MATH: D] and [MATH: E] are both equidistant from the endpoints of [MATH: \overline{AB}.] Therefore, [MATH: D] and [MATH: E] both lie on the perpendicular bisector of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Since only one line can be drawn through two given points, the line [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{DE}] is the perpendicular bisector of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

In particular, we have that [MATH: AC=BC.] We can use this equation to solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: AC|= BC; 3x + 2|= 5x − 2; 4|= 2x; x|= 2]

items.readable_text:
Content:
The most important property of perpendicular lines is the following.

Content:
> Given a line [MATH: l] and a point [MATH: P], there is one and only one line [MATH: m] that passes through [MATH: P] and is perpendicular to [MATH: l].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f5dbcae901ecbd915c2540ec7d4648fa]

Content:
Other nice properties include the following:

Content:
- If two distinct lines are perpendicular to the same (third) line, then these two lines are parallel. For example, in the figure below, both lines [MATH: n] and [MATH: m] are perpendicular to the line [MATH: l]. As a result, [MATH: n \parallel m].
- If a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then that line is also perpendicular to the second parallel line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/93f4d84a21580859479b327609c17a17]

Content:
Symbol [MATH: \perp]

Content:
Finally, if a line [MATH: p] is perpendicular to a line [MATH: q], we can denote it without words using the symbol [MATH: \perp] (perpendicular), as follows:

Content:
[MATH: p \perp q]

Content:
This reads as "[MATH: p] is perpendicular to [MATH: q]."

Content:
> In a plane, if a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it is on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Content:
For example, in the diagram below, we see that [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}] is perpendicular to [MATH: \overline{AB},] and the point [MATH: D] is equidistant from the endpoints of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/66b019c9609135b41ac4a66d0041c6d1]

Content:
Therefore, we can conclude that [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}] is the perpendicular bisector of [MATH: \overline{AB}.] In particular, we conclude that [MATH: AC = BC.]

Item 11 — Example: Applying the Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem

Example Prompt:
Solve for [MATH: x] in the figure below given that [MATH: AD=BD] and [MATH: AE=BE.]

[IMG: /graphics/67f1b28cb2f6912c00c06c6da21bd587]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
By the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, a point equidistant from the endpoints of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment.

Here, the points [MATH: D] and [MATH: E] are both equidistant from the endpoints of [MATH: \overline{AB}.] Therefore, [MATH: D] and [MATH: E] both lie on the perpendicular bisector of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Since only one line can be drawn through two given points, the line [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{DE}] is the perpendicular bisector of [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

In particular, we have that [MATH: AC=BC.] We can use this equation to solve for [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: AC|= BC; 3x + 2|= 5x − 2; 4|= 2x; x|= 2]

Item 14 — Tutorial: Basic Properties of Perpendicular Lines

Content:
The most important property of perpendicular lines is the following.

Content:
> Given a line [MATH: l] and a point [MATH: P], there is one and only one line [MATH: m] that passes through [MATH: P] and is perpendicular to [MATH: l].

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f5dbcae901ecbd915c2540ec7d4648fa]

Content:
Other nice properties include the following:

Content:
- If two distinct lines are perpendicular to the same (third) line, then these two lines are parallel. For example, in the figure below, both lines [MATH: n] and [MATH: m] are perpendicular to the line [MATH: l]. As a result, [MATH: n \parallel m].
- If a line is perpendicular to one of two parallel lines, then that line is also perpendicular to the second parallel line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/93f4d84a21580859479b327609c17a17]

Content:
Symbol [MATH: \perp]

Content:
Finally, if a line [MATH: p] is perpendicular to a line [MATH: q], we can denote it without words using the symbol [MATH: \perp] (perpendicular), as follows:

Content:
[MATH: p \perp q]

Content:
This reads as "[MATH: p] is perpendicular to [MATH: q]."
